lesson_title: Grip, Slopes and the Push That Isn't the Weight
hook_text: On a hill, the ground does NOT push back with your full weight. That one fact is half the marks.
clip_script: Push a heavy wardrobe. Nothing. Push harder. Nothing. Push harder again — and it lurches, and suddenly it is easy. That whole story is friction, and it just told you two secrets. Secret one: while it was standing still, friction was matching you push for push. You gave 150 newtons, it gave 150 back. It only has a limit — and until you beat that limit, nothing moves. Secret two: once it IS moving, the friction is weaker. That's why it got easy. Now put the same crate on a ramp, and here is the thing everybody gets wrong. Gravity still pulls straight down, but the crate can only do two things: slide along the ramp, or press into it. So gravity splits into two piles. Steeper hill, bigger sliding pile, smaller pressing pile — and the ramp pushes back with the SMALLER one. Less pressing means less grip. That is why steep gravel roads lose traction. And the quick test for whether anything slips? Compare the tangent of the slope angle to the grip number. No mass needed. Bigger tangent, it slides.
visual_style: A wardrobe refusing to move, then lurching; cut to a crate on a tilting ramp with gravity's arrow visibly splitting into two glowing components as the angle steepens; final beat on a gravel pass.
mood: Hands-on and slightly conspiratorial — sharing the trick examiners rely on.
pacing: Three failed pushes as a rhythm, slow reveal on the splitting arrow, quick punch to finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and never write N equals mg on a slope again.
